query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐processing treatment that transforms the smooth, continuously straight lamellar interfaces in eutectic high‐entropy alloys into a serrated (tortuous) morphology will both impede micro‐crack initiation/propagation and promote additional strain hardening, thereby raising tensile strength and simultaneously improving room‐temperature ductility relative to the unmodified (smooth‐interface) baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high‐entropy alloy characterized by dual-phase lamellar colonies with smooth, straight internal boundaries that are prone to microcrack initiation under tensile loading at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored post‐processing protocol (e.g., a combination of a precise annealing treatment and/or slight deformation) designed specifically to induce serration of the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on samples processed under identical conditions aside from the additional interface‐modifying post-treatment; microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM) should confirm the formation of serrated boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Transformed (serrated) phase boundaries within the dual-phase lamellar microstructure that create a more tortuous crack path.
generation.mechanism: The serrated interfaces blunt and deflect stress concentrations at the internal colony boundaries, delaying microcrack initiation and propagation; concurrently, the irregular boundary topography promotes strain delocalization and additional strain hardening, thus coupling strength enhancement with improved ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline with smooth lamellar interfaces, the treated alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with increased tensile elongation at fracture.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with as‐cast, smooth dual-phase lamellar colonies that show limited room-temperature tensile ductility due to early microcrack propagation along straight interphase boundaries.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective in eutectic, lamellar high‐entropy alloys where the microstructure is amenable to controlled interface modification; its benefit may be limited if the alloy does not display a clearly defined lamellar morphology or if the heat‐treatment parameters cannot reliably induce serration.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thermal/deformation processing parameters required for consistent serration and the magnitude of the strength/ductility improvements need to be experimentally determined; additionally, the trade-off with any potential microstructural coarsening is not yet fully known.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition. One set remains in the as-cast condition (with smooth lamellar interfaces), while the other is subjected to the controlled post-processing treatment designed to induce serrated interfaces. Confirm the change in interface morphology using scanning electron microscopy. Then conduct standardized room-temperature tensile tests on both sets and statistically compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and tensile elongation.
measurements: Interface morphology characterization (e.g., SEM imaging and quantification of serration amplitude/frequency)
Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and tensile ductility (elongation) from room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-processed samples with serrated interfaces do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (for example, improvement >10% in both strength and ductility metrics) over the as-cast baseline, or if microcrack initiation/propagation is not delayed as seen by fractography, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors. For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys,. However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures,. Developing alloys with ultrahigh strength and excellent ductility simultaneously over a wide temperature range is crucial for developing high-temperature steam turbines [,,]. Recently, as a category of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), dual-phase high-entropy alloys (DP-HEAs) with a soft FCC phase and hard BCC (B2) phase have been reported to have excellent strength–ductility synergy at ambient temperature and high temperature [,,,,,,,,,], and thus have great potential to be used as steam turbine hot end components. Unfortunately, due to the rapid softening of the phase with the BCC structure at high temperatures, the yield strength of the alloy will significantly decrease [,,,,,]. Moreover, due to the weakness of grain boundaries and phase boundaries, the cracks initiate rapidly and propagate along the interface during high-temperature deformation, severely limiting the high-temperature application of FCC/B2 dual-phase high-entropy alloys [,,,,].

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Another possible approach to resolve the hot ductility loss is to introduce serrated grain boundary (SEGB) [], it usually involves a post heat treatment step to induce interactions between mobile grain boundaries and second phases, including carbides [], δ phase [], or γ′ phase []. SEGB has been reported to impede intergranular crack propagation [,,], improve the tensile properties of Ni-based superalloys fabricated by SLM [], and also the ductility of Ni46.23Co23Cr10Fe5Al8.5Ti4W2Mo1C0.15B0.1Zr0.02 fabricated by arc melting []. In this study, we have unprecedentedly utilized SEGB on an HEA fabricated by SLM. This work is the first to investigate the underlying mechanism of hot ductility drop of a HEA fabricated by SLM and study the effect of SEGB on its high temperature tensile and creep properties.
